A1.justification: Both PDFs describe iTool, and all pages, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable. Visual inspection confirms that v1's empty ToolBench panel, leaderboard placeholder and incomplete result rows are document omissions rather than extraction failures.

before.justification: v1 reports original BFCL and API-Bank evaluations, component ablations, curriculum comparisons and iteration analyses, despite several unfinished appendix elements.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and reports additional error analysis, an MCTS ablation and completed evaluations across multiple base models.

M1.justification: v1 Section 4.3 uses reference-based DPO; v2 Section 3.2 adopts reference-free SimPO with length normalization and a reward margin. Replay-buffer initialization also changes from a leave-one-out strategy to random 50% sampling. These alter central training procedures, although v2 retains inconsistent DPO labels in its introduction and architecture figure.

E1.justification: Reported auxiliary training coverage narrows from ToolACE and ToolBench in v1 Section 5.4 to ToolACE alone in v2, explicitly acknowledged in its limitations. However, v1's ToolBench panel already contains no results. The principal BFCL and API-Bank task coverage remains.

E2.justification: v2 adds a comparison against a four-response, probability-ranked alternative to MCTS in Figure 7. The benchmark comparator lists in Tables 1–2 and the DPO, SimPO, IPO and ORPO comparison set remain unchanged; replacing DeepSeek with Gemini in the baseline prose does not establish a comparator change.

E3.justification: The reported ToolACE allocation changes from 90% warm-up plus the remaining 10% for RL to 90% warm-up and 50% for RL. The QLoRA learning rate changes from 5e-5 to an RL rate of 1e-6. The scaling analysis switches from BFCL-v2 to full BFCL, and the plotted iteration range contracts from 0–7 to 0–5.

E4.justification: v2 adds an error-type analysis, an explicit test of MCTS against direct response sampling, and preference-pair case studies. It completes the previously unsupported cross-backbone analysis in Table 3 and revises iteration and scaling analyses. The existing preference-optimizer comparison moves to Appendix B.2 rather than being newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 Table 5 newly specifies MCTS seed 42. Both versions already display error bars in the component ablation without explaining their statistical meaning. Neither provides repeated-training-run counts or significance testing, so this is limited seed disclosure rather than evidence of increased replication.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces iTool's 62.12 overall accuracy and second-place rank with 62.92 and first place; Multi-turn changes from 22.38 to 23.84, while relevance falls from 86.29 to 84.90. These accompany changed training settings. Table 3 fills missing SFT/iTool results, including iTool scores of 60.41 and 63.22 for Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-7B. New analyses add results; API-Bank Table 2 remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 10–11 replace DPO's reference-policy reward and objective with SimPO's length-normalized reward and margin-based objective, changing the mathematical definitions. The task formalization and MCTS equations otherwise retain their substance, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 frames deficiency broadly as poor performance in complex scenarios. v2's abstract and introduction instead identify insufficient data diversity as an underlying problem, define deficiencies as localized response errors, and claim MCTS exploration addresses diversity. It also adds an approximately 3% same-size-model advantage and drops v1's broad introductory claim of generalization across varied synthetic datasets.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantive internal/external-factor explanation, attributes excessive-iteration degradation to overfitting and reduced diversity, and acknowledges possible sacrifices on simpler Non-live cases. Its limitations replace v1's 'todo' with discussion of MCTS cost, performance compromises from search constraints, untested larger backbones and reliance on one synthetic dataset.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the fragmentary implementation appendix with training and search settings, hyperparameter searches, preference-filtering thresholds, checkpoint selection, LLaMA-Factory information and a substantially expanded evaluation prompt. Hardware/time reporting changes from four A100 GPUs within 20 hours to eight V100 GPUs within 28 hours. Much of this is newly disclosed detail rather than demonstrated procedural change.

R1.justification: v2 adds QLoRA, LLaMA-Factory and Xiong et al.'s iterative preference-learning work, while removing references including Rosset et al., the GPT-4 report and DeepSeek-V3. Related work broadens its framing from preference optimization to reinforcement learning, but the principal positioning around synthetic tool data and iterative preference learning remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. Task overview becomes part of an early Problem Statement and Analysis section, related work moves after experiments, and preference-optimizer analysis moves into an expanded appendix. The title and author block also change. This substantially reorganizes the narrative beyond ordinary copyediting.

P2.justification: v2 adds tool-interaction, error-analysis, MCTS-ablation and search-tree figures, plus implementation and preference-example tables. Scaling and optimizer plots are redesigned; the latter moves to the appendix and omits the previous task-breakdown bars. The empty leaderboard placeholder disappears, while the original weather example is retained and reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important deficiencies in v1: missing cross-backbone results, largely unfinished implementation documentation and placeholder limitations. The MCTS control and concrete error analysis substantially strengthen empirical support and make the procedure easier to reproduce. Diversity-related causal claims remain only indirectly supported, and inconsistent DPO/SimPO labeling persists, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in completeness and assessability.
